newsitem.title: USA: U.S. CRUDE OUTLOOK - RANGEBOUND ON IRAQ, GASOLINE.
newsitem.headline: U.S. CRUDE OUTLOOK - RANGEBOUND ON IRAQ, GASOLINE.

text.p: U.S. crude oil prices are expected to hover in a wide range this week, with attention drawn to renewed Iraqi exports and gasoline prices, analysts said on Monday.
Iraqi Oil Minister Amir Muhammed Rasheed said on Monday that exports will resume within two days under the second phase of the oil-for-food deal with the United Nations.
The minister said Baghdad planned to export 30 million barrels of crude by the end of August from Ceyhan and Mina al-Bakr, equivalent to some 1.5 million barrels per day (bpd).

The market seemed to shrug off the news in early trading. September light sweet crude on the New York Mercantile Exchange (NYMEX) was trading at $19.70 a barrel at 1114 EST/1514 GMT, up 16 cents from Friday's settlement.
"We're going to see plenty of Iraqi crude in the next couple of weeks, but the market still seems to be ignoring it," said Tom Bentz, head of the energy division at High Yield Analytics in New York.
"Once it starts showing up, displacing other crudes . . . we'll start to see the impact," he said.
The market's other focus is gasoline, which could witness one last hurrah before winding down for heating oil season, analysts said.
"The fate of the market hangs just as much on gasoline as on Iraq," said William Brown, president of W.H. Brown and Co in New York.
After weakening toward the end of last week, September unleaded gasoline was trading at 62 cents a gallon at 1122 EDT/1522 GMT on the NYMEX, up slightly from Friday.
"I think there's a risk we come down to 60 cents," said Brown. "If we get down to $19.00 on crude and 60 cents on gasoline, that'll be the bottom then we'll go up and come down harder."
Bentz pegged the week's range at $19.50 to $20.25 a barrel. If $19.50 is broken, the next level of support is around $19.00-19.20.

On the cash side of the crude market, domestic grade traders in the U.S. Gulf expected weakening sour differentials to key this week's activity. Oversupply concerns depressed West Texas Sour/Midland barrels late last week to around a $1.50-55 discount against September benchmark WTI/Cushing.

Iraqi crude contracts with U.S. companies Bayoil and Coastal were seen as the main weight on Gulf domestics. Barring any late changes, both companies, along with Chevron, were seen loading Iraqi crudes in the next few weeks for destinations in the Atlantic Basin.
"The way it looks I wouldn't be surprised if the WTS diff goes down to around $1.70-80 under WTI. I never understood why it was trading at $1.25-35 in the first place," said a Texas trader.

Sweet cash barrels hung on to a slight, but evaporating, premium to September WTI/Cushing. Light Louisiana Sweet/St. James has lost more than 15 cents a barrel in the previous week or so to move at only a 12-15 cents premium.

Cheapening North Sea Brent barrels have cut into the LLS premium, though the WTI/Brent spread has tightened to only $1.15-25 for September and to $1.15-25 for October. Dated Brent, however, is running at around 25 cents a barrel under the September quote, encouraging Brent offers into the Gulf.
"The more people look at the supply in tanks and what is fixed to come over, they see no need to worry about finding cheap crude," said a cash dealer.
